topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Temperature and particle motion
topics.description: Explain that particles in every substance are constantly moving, and that the temperature of a substance is a measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles — hotter means faster-moving (or more strongly vibrating) particles
evidence: States that particles move faster on average when a substance is heated
Describes particle motion in a solid (vibrating in place), liquid (sliding past) and gas (fast, random, far apart)
Explains why a drop of food colouring spreads faster in hot water than in cold water
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} drops food colouring into a glass of hot water and a glass of cold water, can they explain — using moving particles — why it spreads faster in the hot one?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Diffusion and particle movement
topics.description: Explain diffusion — the spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration — as a result of random particle motion, and explain why it is fastest in gases and in warmer conditions
evidence: Defines diffusion as net movement from high to low concentration
Explains why a smell spreads across a room without anyone fanning it
Predicts that diffusion is faster in gases than liquids, and faster when warmer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If someone opens a bottle of perfume at one end of a room, can {{name}} explain why people at the other end smell it a little later, using the idea of moving particles?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Gas pressure from particle collisions
topics.description: Explain gas pressure as the result of gas particles colliding with the walls of their container, and predict how pressure changes when the gas is heated, compressed or more gas is added
evidence: Explains that pressure comes from many particle collisions with the container walls
Predicts that heating a sealed container raises the pressure because particles hit the walls harder and more often
Explains why pumping more air into a tyre makes it firmer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pumps up a bike tyre, can they explain what the air particles inside are doing to make the tyre feel harder?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Why heating curves have flat sections
topics.description: Explain the shape of temperature–time graphs for a substance being heated or cooled: on the sloping sections energy speeds up particles (temperature rises), while on the flat sections energy is used to overcome the attractions between particles and change their arrangement, so temperature stays constant until the change of state is complete
evidence: Identifies melting and boiling points from the flat sections of a heating curve
Labels which state(s) are present on each section of the curve
Explains why the temperature does not rise while ice is melting even though it is still being heated
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a graph of ice being heated until it boils, can they point to where it is melting and explain why the line goes flat there?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Evaporation causes cooling
topics.description: Explain that during evaporation the fastest-moving particles escape from the surface of a liquid, lowering the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind — which is why sweating and wet skin cool us down
evidence: Distinguishes evaporation (at the surface, any temperature) from boiling (throughout, at the boiling point)
Explains cooling by evaporation in terms of the most energetic particles leaving
Lists factors that speed up evaporation (temperature, surface area, airflow)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets out of a swimming pool on a windy day and feels cold, can they explain why the evaporating water makes their skin cooler?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Calculating density
topics.description: Calculate density using density = mass ÷ volume, measure the density of regular and irregular objects (by displacement), and use particle spacing to explain why gases are far less dense than solids and liquids
evidence: Calculates density from mass and volume with correct units (g/cm³ or kg/m³)
Finds the volume of an irregular object by water displacement
Predicts whether an object will float in water by comparing densities
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a 50 g pebble that pushes the water level in a measuring cylinder up by 20 cm³, can they work out the pebble's density and say whether it will float?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Strengths and limits of the particle model
topics.description: Evaluate the simple particle model: recognise what it explains well (states, diffusion, pressure) and what it leaves out — particles are not hard coloured spheres, there are forces between them, and real particles are atoms, ions or molecules of different sizes
evidence: Names two things the particle model explains well
Names at least two simplifications in particle diagrams (e.g. no forces shown, particles drawn as identical spheres)
Explains why scientists still use a model they know is simplified
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a textbook particle diagram of a gas, can they say one thing it gets right and one way real gas particles are different from the picture?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Kelvin scale and absolute zero
topics.description: Explain absolute zero (0 K, about −273 °C) as the temperature at which particles have the least possible kinetic energy, and convert between degrees Celsius and kelvin
evidence: Converts temperatures between °C and K by adding or subtracting 273
Explains why there is no temperature below absolute zero using particle motion
Explains why the Kelvin scale has no negative values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told that liquid nitrogen boils at about 77 K, can they convert that to degrees Celsius and explain what 0 K would mean for the particles?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Specific latent heat
topics.description: Use the idea that changing state needs energy without a temperature change, and calculate the energy for a change of state using E = mL, distinguishing specific latent heat of fusion from vaporisation
evidence: Explains that energy during a change of state breaks or weakens forces between particles rather than raising temperature
Calculates energy needed to melt or boil a given mass using E = mL
Explains why a scald from steam is worse than from boiling water at the same temperature
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows it takes 334 000 J to melt 1 kg of ice, can they work out the energy to melt a 0.2 kg ice cube and explain why the thermometer doesn't rise while it melts?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Gas laws: pressure, volume and temperature
topics.description: Describe and use the relationships between pressure, volume and temperature for a fixed mass of gas — pressure × volume is constant at constant temperature (Boyle's law), and volume or pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature — explaining each with particle collisions
evidence: Uses p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ to find a new pressure or volume
Explains why the temperature must be in kelvin for proportional relationships
Explains each law using the frequency and force of particle collisions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} squeezes a sealed syringe of air to half its volume, can they predict what happens to the pressure and explain it in terms of the particles?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Charges and masses of subatomic particles
topics.description: Describe the atom as a tiny positively charged nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons, and give the relative charge and relative mass of each particle
evidence: Gives relative charges: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1
Gives relative masses: proton 1, neutron 1, electron about 1/2000
Explains why an atom has no overall charge
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why an atom with 6 protons isn't positively charged overall, can they explain the role of the electrons?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Atomic number and mass number
topics.description: Use atomic number (number of protons) and mass number (protons + neutrons) to work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom from its nuclear symbol
evidence: Reads atomic and mass numbers from a nuclear symbol or periodic table
Calculates neutrons as mass number − atomic number
Explains that the atomic number identifies the element
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees sodium written as ²³₁₁Na, can they work out how many protons, neutrons and electrons a sodium atom has?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Isotopes
topics.description: Explain that isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers but almost identical chemical properties
evidence: Defines isotope correctly
Works out neutron numbers for isotopes such as carbon-12 and carbon-14
Explains why isotopes react (almost) the same way chemically, using electron arrangement
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told about carbon-12 and carbon-14, can they explain what is the same and what is different about these two kinds of carbon atom?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Relative atomic mass
topics.description: Calculate relative atomic mass as the weighted mean mass of an element's isotopes using their percentage abundances, and explain why values like chlorine's 35.5 are not whole numbers
evidence: Calculates a weighted mean from isotope masses and abundances
Explains why chlorine's relative atomic mass is 35.5
Locates relative atomic masses on a periodic table
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37, can they show why its relative atomic mass is 35.5?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: How the model of the atom developed
topics.description: Trace how evidence changed the model of the atom — Dalton's solid spheres, Thomson's plum pudding, Rutherford's gold-foil experiment revealing the nucleus, Bohr's electron shells and Chadwick's discovery of the neutron
evidence: Puts the main atomic models in historical order
Explains what the gold-foil results showed and why the plum pudding model had to change
Uses the story as an example of models being revised by new evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that most alpha particles went straight through gold foil but a few bounced back, can they explain what this told Rutherford about the atom?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Electron shells and configurations
topics.description: Write electron configurations for the first 20 elements using the 2, 8, 8 filling pattern and draw shell diagrams, linking the number of outer-shell electrons to the element's position
evidence: Writes configurations such as 2,8,1 for sodium
Draws a shell diagram for an atom given its atomic number
Identifies the number of outer-shell electrons
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told magnesium has 12 electrons, can they draw how those electrons are arranged in shells?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The size of atoms and nuclei
topics.description: Appreciate the scale of atoms (about 10⁻¹⁰ m across) and nuclei (about 10⁻¹⁴ to 10⁻¹⁵ m), using scientific notation and analogies to show that an atom is mostly empty space
evidence: Writes the size of an atom in scientific notation
Compares atomic and nuclear radii as a ratio (about 10 000 to 100 000 times)
Uses an analogy (e.g. a pea in a stadium) for the nucleus inside an atom
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told an atom is about 0.0000000001 m across, can they write that in scientific notation and describe how small the nucleus is by comparison?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Periodic table patterns from electrons
topics.description: Explain the structure of the periodic table in terms of electrons — group number matches the number of outer-shell electrons (for main groups) and period number matches the number of occupied shells — and use this to predict similar properties within a group
evidence: Links group number to outer-shell electrons for main-group elements
Links period number to number of shells
Predicts that elements in the same group react similarly because they have the same number of outer electrons
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told an unfamiliar element is in Group 2, Period 4, can they say how many outer electrons and shells it has, and which element it will behave like?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Alkali metals (Group 1)
topics.description: Describe the properties and reactions of the alkali metals with water and oxygen, and explain why reactivity increases down the group using distance of the outer electron from the nucleus
evidence: Describes lithium, sodium and potassium reacting with water and names the products
States that reactivity increases down Group 1
Explains the trend in terms of the outer electron being lost more easily
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has seen lithium fizz gently in water and potassium burst into flame, can they predict what rubidium would do and explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Halogens (Group 7)
topics.description: Describe the halogens' physical trends and displacement reactions, and explain why reactivity decreases down the group because it becomes harder to gain an electron
evidence: Describes colour and state trend from fluorine to iodine
Predicts whether a halogen will displace another from a salt solution
Explains decreasing reactivity in terms of attracting an extra electron
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} adds chlorine water to potassium bromide solution, can they predict what happens and explain why chlorine wins?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Noble gases and stable outer shells
topics.description: Explain that the noble gases are unreactive because their outer shell is full, and use this to explain why other atoms tend to lose, gain or share electrons
evidence: Explains noble-gas unreactivity in terms of a full outer shell
Gives uses that depend on unreactivity (e.g. argon in light bulbs, helium in balloons)
Links full outer shells to how other atoms form bonds
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why balloons are filled with helium rather than hydrogen, can they connect helium's safety to its electron arrangement?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Trends across a period
topics.description: Describe and explain trends in atomic radius and in how easily atoms lose electrons across a period and down a group, using nuclear charge and shielding qualitatively
evidence: States that atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group
Explains the trend using increasing nuclear charge with the same number of shells
Uses the trends to compare the reactivity of two main-group elements
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares sodium and chlorine in the same row of the periodic table, can they explain why chlorine's atoms are smaller even though they have more electrons?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Forming ions
topics.description: Explain that atoms become ions by losing or gaining electrons to achieve a full outer shell, predict the charge on simple ions from group number, and draw ions with square brackets and charges
evidence: Predicts ion charges for groups 1, 2, 6 and 7
Draws electron diagrams for ions such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻
Explains that metals form positive ions and non-metals negative ions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked what happens to a magnesium atom when it forms an ion, can they say how many electrons it loses and what charge it ends up with?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Ionic bonding and lattices
topics.description: Explain ionic bonding as the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice, and use this to explain high melting points and conductivity when molten or dissolved
evidence: Draws a dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride
Explains high melting point in terms of many strong attractions in the lattice
Explains why ionic compounds conduct only when molten or in solution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why salt has to be melted or dissolved before it conducts electricity, can they explain what the ions need to be able to do?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Covalent bonding
topics.description: Explain covalent bonding as a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms, and draw dot-and-cross and displayed diagrams for simple molecules such as H₂, H₂O, CH₄ and CO₂
evidence: Draws dot-and-cross diagrams for simple molecules
Identifies single and double bonds
Explains that covalent bonds form between non-metal atoms
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a water molecule, can they show which electrons are shared between the oxygen and the two hydrogens?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Properties of simple molecular substances
topics.description: Explain why simple molecular substances such as water, oxygen and methane have low melting and boiling points: the covalent bonds inside molecules are strong, but the forces between molecules are weak
evidence: Distinguishes bonds within molecules from forces between molecules
Explains low boiling points using weak intermolecular forces
Explains why simple molecular substances do not conduct electricity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why water boils at only 100 °C when covalent bonds are strong, can they explain what actually gets overcome when water boils?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Giant covalent structures
topics.description: Explain the properties of giant covalent structures — diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide — in terms of networks of strong covalent bonds, including why graphite conducts and is soft while diamond is hard
evidence: Explains the very high melting points of giant covalent structures
Explains graphite's conductivity using delocalised electrons
Contrasts the hardness of diamond with the slipperiness of graphite layers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why pencil 'lead' (graphite) leaves marks on paper while diamond can cut glass — though both are pure carbon — can they explain using structure?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Metallic bonding
topics.description: Explain metallic bonding as positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, and use it to explain conductivity, malleability and why alloys are harder than pure metals
evidence: Draws and labels a model of metallic bonding
Explains electrical conductivity of metals using delocalised electrons
Explains why alloys are harder using disrupted layers of ions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why copper wire can be bent without snapping and also carries electricity, can they explain both using the structure of the metal?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Inferring bonding from bulk properties
topics.description: Use bulk properties — melting and boiling point, conductivity, solubility, hardness — to infer the type of structure and strength of forces between particles in an unknown substance
evidence: Classifies an unknown substance as ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent or metallic from data
Ranks substances by strength of forces between particles using melting/boiling points
Plans a simple test to distinguish two structures
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a white solid that melts at 801 °C and conducts only when dissolved, can they decide what kind of structure it has and justify it?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Molecular structure in designed materials
topics.description: Explain how the molecular-level structure of designed materials — long-chain polymers, alloys, conducting metals, nanoparticles — determines how they function, and communicate this clearly
evidence: Explains why polymers made of long tangled chains are flexible but strong
Explains why electrical wiring is metal using structure
Writes a short technical explanation linking a material's structure to a use
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why plastic bags stretch rather than snap, can they explain it in terms of the long molecules the plastic is made from?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Writing formulae of ionic compounds
topics.description: Work out the formula of an ionic compound by balancing the charges on its ions, including compound ions such as sulfate, nitrate and hydroxide
evidence: Writes formulae such as MgCl₂ and Al₂O₃ from ion charges
Uses brackets correctly for compound ions, e.g. Ca(OH)₂
Explains why the total charge in the formula must be zero
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows calcium forms Ca²⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, can they work out the formula of calcium chloride and explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Counting atoms in formulae and equations
topics.description: Count the atoms of each element in chemical formulae and equations, correctly handling subscripts, brackets and the large numbers (coefficients) written in front of formulae
evidence: Counts atoms of each element in formulae such as H₂SO₄ and Ca(OH)₂
Distinguishes 2H₂O (two molecules) from H₂O₂ (a different substance)
Names simple compounds from their formulae
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the formula H₂SO₄, can they say which elements are in it and how many atoms of each there are?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Word equations
topics.description: Write and interpret word equations for chemical reactions, identifying reactants and products and using the arrow to mean 'react to form'
evidence: Writes a word equation for a described reaction
Identifies reactants and products in a given equation
Explains that the arrow is not an equals sign
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees magnesium burning brightly to make a white powder, can they write a word equation for what happened?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reactions rearrange atoms
topics.description: Explain that in a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged into new substances but none are created or destroyed, using particle diagrams of reactants and products to show why total mass is conserved
evidence: Draws before-and-after particle diagrams with the same atoms
Explains conservation of mass in terms of atoms
Distinguishes new substances formed from the same atoms
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a particle picture of hydrogen and oxygen making water, can they show that every atom at the start is still there at the end?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Balancing chemical equations
topics.description: Balance symbol equations by changing only the numbers in front of formulae so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides
evidence: Balances equations such as Mg + O₂ → MgO and CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
Explains why subscripts must not be changed
Checks a balanced equation by counting atoms of each element
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, can they balance it and explain why they can't just change H₂O to H₂O₂?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: State symbols
topics.description: Add state symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) to equations and use them to tell, for example, which product is a gas that escapes or a precipitate that forms
evidence: Adds correct state symbols to a balanced equation
Explains that (aq) means dissolved in water
Uses state symbols to spot a precipitate or gas
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), can they say which product bubbles out of the beaker?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Mass changes in open and closed systems
topics.description: Explain why mass seems to change when a reaction happens in an open container (a gas escapes or is gained from the air) but stays the same in a sealed container
evidence: Predicts the mass change when a gas is produced in an open flask
Explains why metal gains mass when heated in air
Designs a closed-system test to show conservation of mass
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} weighs a fizzing tablet dissolving in an open cup and sees the mass go down, can they explain why mass hasn't really been destroyed?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Relative formula mass
topics.description: Calculate the relative formula mass of a compound by adding the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in its formula
evidence: Calculates Mr for compounds like CO₂ and Ca(OH)₂
Uses brackets in formulae correctly when counting atoms
Calculates the percentage by mass of an element in a compound
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told carbon has relative atomic mass 12 and oxygen 16, can they work out the relative formula mass of carbon dioxide?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The mole
topics.description: Understand the mole as a fixed number of particles (6.02 × 10²³, the Avogadro constant), and convert between mass, moles and relative formula mass
evidence: Uses moles = mass ÷ Mr in both directions
Explains why chemists count particles in moles
Uses the Avogadro constant to find a number of particles
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 36 g of water (Mr 18), can they work out how many moles that is and roughly how many molecules?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Calculating reacting masses
topics.description: Use a balanced equation and moles to calculate the mass of product formed or reactant needed, showing that atoms and mass are conserved mathematically
evidence: Uses mole ratios from a balanced equation
Calculates the mass of product from a given mass of reactant
Checks that the total mass of reactants equals total mass of products
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} burns 12 g of carbon completely, can they use C + O₂ → CO₂ to work out the mass of carbon dioxide made?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Limiting reactants and percentage yield
topics.description: Identify the limiting reactant in a mixture, explain why the other is in excess, and calculate theoretical and percentage yield
evidence: Identifies the limiting reactant from given masses
Calculates percentage yield from actual and theoretical yield
Gives reasons why actual yield is less than theoretical
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} makes sandwiches with 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese, can they use that idea to explain what a limiting reactant is in a chemical reaction?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Concentration of solutions
topics.description: Calculate the concentration of a solution in g/dm³ and mol/dm³, and explain how dilution changes concentration but not the amount of solute
evidence: Calculates concentration from mass or moles and volume
Converts cm³ to dm³
Explains dilution in terms of the same solute in more solvent
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} dissolves 20 g of salt in 500 cm³ of water, can they work out the concentration in grams per dm³?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Predicting reaction outcomes from the periodic table
topics.description: Predict and explain the products of simple reactions between main-group elements (e.g. sodium and chlorine, carbon and oxygen) using outer-electron arrangements and periodic trends
evidence: Predicts the product and formula of a Group 1 metal reacting with a halogen
Explains the outcome using electron transfer or sharing
Predicts which of two similar reactions will be more vigorous
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked what forms when potassium reacts with bromine, can they predict the product, write its formula and say why it forms?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Combustion of fuels
topics.description: Describe complete combustion of hydrocarbon fuels to carbon dioxide and water, incomplete combustion producing carbon monoxide and soot, and why incomplete combustion is dangerous
evidence: Writes a word and symbol equation for the complete combustion of methane
States the products of incomplete combustion
Explains why carbon monoxide alarms are needed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a gas flame burning yellow and sooty instead of blue, can they explain what is different about how the fuel is burning and why it matters?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Oxidation and reduction as electron transfer
topics.description: Define oxidation as loss of electrons and reduction as gain of electrons, identify what is oxidised and reduced in displacement reactions, and connect this to extracting metals
evidence: Identifies oxidation and reduction in a displacement reaction
Writes half-equations for simple metal/ion changes
Explains why carbon can extract iron but not aluminium from their oxides
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} puts an iron nail in copper sulfate solution and it turns pink, can they explain which substance lost electrons and which gained them?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Electrolysis of ionic compounds
topics.description: Explain electrolysis as using electricity to break down a molten or dissolved ionic compound, predicting which ions move to each electrode and what forms there
evidence: Explains why the compound must be molten or dissolved
Predicts products at each electrode for a molten binary compound
Explains why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than with carbon
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} passes electricity through molten lead bromide, can they predict what appears at each electrode and explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Acids, alkalis and hydrogen ions
topics.description: Explain acids as sources of H⁺ ions and alkalis as sources of OH⁻ ions in solution, write the ionic equation for neutralisation, and understand that each pH unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration
evidence: Writes H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O for neutralisation
Explains that pH 3 has ten times the H⁺ concentration of pH 4
Distinguishes strong from dilute acids
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares lemon juice at pH 2 with vinegar at pH 3, can they say how many times more hydrogen ions the lemon juice has?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Designing a hand warmer or cold pack
topics.description: Design, test and refine a device that uses an exothermic or endothermic process to warm or cool, choosing amounts of substances and measuring temperature change to evaluate the design
evidence: Chooses an exothermic or endothermic reaction suitable for the purpose
Measures temperature change and compares designs fairly
Suggests one change to improve the device and justifies it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to make an instant cold pack for a sports injury, can they choose a suitable reaction and describe how they'd test which mix works best?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Bond energies and energy change
topics.description: Explain that breaking bonds takes in energy and making bonds releases energy, so whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic depends on the balance of total bond energies
evidence: States that bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic
Explains an exothermic reaction as releasing more energy making bonds than breaking them
Calculates an overall energy change from given bond energies
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked where the energy of burning methane comes from, can they explain it in terms of bonds broken and bonds made?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reaction profiles and activation energy
topics.description: Draw and interpret reaction profile diagrams showing the energy of reactants and products, the overall energy change and the activation energy, including the effect of a catalyst
evidence: Draws profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions
Labels activation energy and overall energy change
Shows how a catalyst lowers activation energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown an energy diagram where the products are lower than the reactants, can they say whether the reaction heats or cools its surroundings and point out the activation energy?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Collision theory
topics.description: Explain that reactions happen only when particles collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy), so the rate depends on the frequency and energy of collisions
evidence: States the two conditions for a successful collision
Explains why not every collision leads to a reaction
Links particle speed to collision energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why food goes off more slowly in the fridge, can they explain using collisions between particles?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Factors affecting the rate of reaction
topics.description: Explain how temperature, concentration (or gas pressure), surface area and catalysts change the rate of a reaction, in terms of the frequency and energy of collisions
evidence: Predicts the effect of each factor on rate
Explains each effect with collision theory
Explains why powdered solids react faster than lumps
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} drops a whole indigestion tablet and a crushed one into water, can they predict which fizzes away faster and explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Measuring rates from graphs
topics.description: Measure the rate of a reaction by tracking mass lost or gas produced over time, plot the results and use the gradient to compare rates, including the gradient of a tangent for an instantaneous rate
evidence: Plans an experiment to collect gas volume over time
Calculates mean rate as change in quantity ÷ time
Explains why the curve levels off as the reaction finishes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} plots the volume of gas from a reaction every 10 seconds, can they use the graph to tell when the reaction was fastest and when it stopped?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
topics.description: Explain that some reactions are reversible and that in a closed system they reach dynamic equilibrium, where the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates so amounts stay constant
evidence: Uses the ⇌ symbol correctly
Explains why equilibrium is 'dynamic' rather than stopped
Gives an example of a reversible reaction (e.g. heating hydrated copper sulfate)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees blue copper sulfate turn white when heated and blue again when water is added, can they explain what makes this reaction reversible?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Shifting equilibrium (Le Chatelier's principle)
topics.description: Predict how changing concentration, temperature or pressure shifts the position of an equilibrium, and use this to refine conditions that increase the yield of a product (e.g. in the Haber process)
evidence: Predicts the direction of shift when a product is removed
Predicts the effect of temperature on an exothermic equilibrium
Explains the compromise conditions used in an industrial process
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a reaction that makes ammonia gives out heat, can they predict whether cooling it would give more or less ammonia, and why factories don't simply make it very cold?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Inside the nucleus
topics.description: Describe the nucleus as protons and neutrons held together by the strong nuclear force, which overcomes the electrical repulsion between protons at very short range, and recognise that some nuclei are unstable
evidence: Explains why protons in a nucleus should repel each other
Names the strong nuclear force as what holds the nucleus together
Recognises that the balance of neutrons and protons affects stability
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why a nucleus full of positive protons doesn't fly apart, can they explain what holds it together?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Radioactive decay
topics.description: Explain that unstable nuclei decay randomly by emitting radiation — alpha and beta decay change the nucleus into a different element, while gamma emission releases energy without changing the numbers of protons and neutrons — and that we can predict how a large sample behaves but not when one nucleus will decay
evidence: Defines radioactive decay
Explains why decay is random for one nucleus but predictable for many
Explains that alpha and beta decay change one element into another, but gamma emission does not
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a single atom of radon might decay in a second or in a week, can they explain how scientists can still predict what a big sample will do?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
topics.description: Describe alpha particles (helium nuclei), beta particles (fast electrons from the nucleus) and gamma rays (electromagnetic waves), comparing their penetrating power, ionising power and range
evidence: Identifies what each type of radiation is
Ranks the types by penetration (paper, aluminium, lead)
Explains why alpha is most dangerous inside the body but least outside
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a radiation source is stopped by a sheet of paper, can they identify which type it is and explain why it would still be dangerous if swallowed?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Nuclear decay equations
topics.description: Write balanced nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay, showing that the total mass number and total atomic number are conserved even though the element changes
evidence: Writes an alpha decay equation for a given nucleus
Writes a beta decay equation and explains the change in atomic number
Checks that mass numbers and atomic numbers balance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay, can they work out the mass number and atomic number of the nucleus it becomes?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Half-life
topics.description: Define half-life as the time for half the unstable nuclei (or the activity) of a sample to decay, read half-life from a decay graph and calculate how much remains after a number of half-lives
evidence: Reads half-life from an activity–time graph
Calculates the fraction remaining after n half-lives
Explains how half-life makes radiocarbon dating possible
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a sample has a half-life of 6 hours, can they work out what fraction is left after a day?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Nuclear fission and chain reactions
topics.description: Explain nuclear fission as a large nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei and releasing neutrons and energy, and how a controlled chain reaction is used in a nuclear power station
evidence: Describes fission of uranium-235 after absorbing a neutron
Explains a chain reaction and how control rods manage it
Compares nuclear power with fossil fuels
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked what control rods in a nuclear reactor are for, can they explain using the idea of a chain reaction?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Nuclear fusion in stars
topics.description: Explain nuclear fusion as light nuclei joining to make a heavier nucleus, releasing energy, why it needs extremely high temperature and pressure, and that it powers the Sun
evidence: Describes hydrogen nuclei fusing to make helium
Explains why fusion needs very high temperatures (overcoming repulsion)
Contrasts fusion with fission
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how the Sun produces its energy, can they explain fusion and why it needs such a hot core?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The scale of nuclear energy
topics.description: Compare the energy released in nuclear processes with chemical reactions — millions of times more per kilogram — and explain qualitatively that the energy comes from a tiny decrease in mass (E = mc²)
evidence: States that nuclear reactions release far more energy per kg than burning fuel
Explains that nuclear energy comes from a small loss of mass
Explains why protons + neutrons are conserved in nuclear processes even though atoms are not
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that a small pellet of nuclear fuel releases as much energy as a tonne of coal, can they explain where that enormous energy comes from?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Radiation risks and uses
topics.description: Distinguish irradiation from contamination, explain how dose, half-life and type of radiation affect risk, and evaluate uses of radiation in medicine and industry
evidence: Defines irradiation and contamination
Explains how distance, time and shielding reduce exposure
Evaluates a medical use of radiation (e.g. tracers or radiotherapy)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why a hospital tracer should have a short half-life, can they explain the trade-off between doing its job and keeping the patient safe?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Defining a system and its boundary
topics.description: Choose the system being studied, draw its boundary, and track energy flowing into and out of it — recognising that a closed system's total energy stays constant, while an open system can gain or lose energy
evidence: Draws a boundary around a chosen system (e.g. kettle + water)
Identifies energy flows crossing the boundary
Explains how choosing a different boundary changes what counts as 'lost'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is describing a pan of water heating on a stove, can they say what they're counting as 'the system' and which energy transfers go in or out of it?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Energy transfer pathways
topics.description: Identify the four ways energy is transferred between stores — mechanically (by a force doing work), electrically (by a current), by heating, and by radiation (light and other electromagnetic waves) — noting that sound also carries energy as a mechanical wave, and describe a chain of transfers for a familiar device
evidence: Names the four transfer pathways
Describes the stores and pathways in a chain for a device (e.g. torch, kettle)
Distinguishes a store from a pathway
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} switches on a battery torch, can they describe the energy stores and how energy moves between them until it lights the room?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed
topics.description: Explain, using data, that an object's kinetic energy increases with its mass and increases much more steeply with its speed (doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy)
evidence: Predicts which of two objects has more kinetic energy from mass and speed
Interprets a table or graph showing kinetic energy rising faster than speed
Explains why speed limits matter so much for crash damage
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a car at 30 mph with the same car at 60 mph, can they explain why the faster car carries far more than twice the energy?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Calculating kinetic energy
topics.description: Calculate kinetic energy using KE = ½mv², with mass in kg and speed in m/s, and rearrange to find mass or speed
evidence: Calculates KE for given mass and speed with units of joules
Rearranges to find speed from kinetic energy and mass
Explains the effect of doubling speed using the v² term
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a 60 kg cyclist is travelling at 5 m/s, can they work out the cyclist's kinetic energy?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Gravitational potential energy and height
topics.description: Explain that lifting an object stores energy in the gravitational store, and that the amount depends on its mass, its height and the strength of gravity
evidence: Predicts which of two objects stores more gravitational potential energy
Describes energy changing from gravitational to kinetic as an object falls
Explains why the same object would store less energy at the same height on the Moon
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} carries a heavy bag up the stairs, can they explain where the energy they used has gone and how it could be got back?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Calculating gravitational potential energy
topics.description: Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy using ΔGPE = mgh, with g ≈ 9.8 N/kg on Earth, and rearrange to find height or mass
evidence: Calculates GPE change for a lifted object
Rearranges to find the height reached
Uses different values of g for other planets
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} lifts a 2 kg box onto a shelf 1.5 m high, can they calculate how much gravitational potential energy it gained?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Elastic potential energy
topics.description: Calculate the energy stored in a stretched spring using E = ½ke² (within the limit of proportionality) and relate it to the area under a force–extension graph
evidence: Calculates elastic energy from spring constant and extension
Identifies the area under a force–extension graph as stored energy
Explains why the formula only applies up to the limit of proportionality
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stretches a spring with spring constant 200 N/m by 0.1 m, can they work out how much energy it stores?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Energy stored in fields
topics.description: Explain that energy can be stored when objects interact through a field at a distance — gravitational, magnetic or electric — and that this energy changes as the objects move closer or further apart
evidence: Describes energy changes as two magnets are pushed together or pulled apart
Compares energy in an electric field to gravitational potential energy
Draws a simple model of two charged objects and the forces between them
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pushes the like poles of two magnets together and lets go, can they explain where the energy that makes them spring apart was stored?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Energy as motion and position of particles
topics.description: Model the energy of a macroscopic object as the sum of energy from the motion of its particles (kinetic) and their relative positions (potential), explaining thermal energy and changes of state in these terms
evidence: Explains thermal energy as particle kinetic plus potential energy
Explains a change of state as a change in particle potential energy
Describes friction converting kinetic energy into thermal energy of particles
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} rubs their hands together and they get warm, can they explain what has happened to the energy in terms of particles?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Energy conservation calculations
topics.description: Use conservation of energy to solve problems where energy transfers between kinetic and gravitational stores (falling objects, pendulums, roller coasters), such as finding speed from height using mgh = ½mv²
evidence: Equates GPE lost to KE gained for a falling object
Calculates the speed of an object after falling a given height
Explains why real speeds are lower than calculated
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} drops a ball from 5 m, can they use energy ideas to work out how fast it is going just before it hits the ground?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Why dissipated energy is less useful
topics.description: Explain that energy dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings spreads out thinly over many particles, so although none is destroyed it becomes much harder to use again — the idea behind 'wasted' energy
evidence: Identifies where energy is dissipated in a device
Explains why dissipated energy is hard to use again
Explains that dissipation does not break conservation of energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} notices a phone charger getting warm, can they explain what's happening to some of the energy and why it isn't destroyed?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reducing unwanted energy transfers
topics.description: Explain how lubrication, insulation, streamlining and better design reduce unwanted energy transfers and increase efficiency, and evaluate trade-offs such as cost
evidence: Explains how lubrication reduces dissipation by friction
Explains how loft insulation reduces energy transfer from a house
Compares two design improvements by their effect on efficiency
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how to make a bicycle more efficient, can they suggest two changes and explain what wasted energy each one reduces?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The work–energy principle
topics.description: Use the principle that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, and apply it to braking distances and accelerating vehicles
evidence: States the work–energy principle
Calculates a braking force from kinetic energy and stopping distance
Explains why doubling speed roughly quadruples braking distance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a car's speed doubles, can they use energy and work ideas to explain why its braking distance becomes about four times longer?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Energy bills and kilowatt-hours
topics.description: Calculate energy transferred by appliances using E = P × t in both joules and kilowatt-hours, and use unit prices to work out running costs
evidence: Calculates energy in kWh from power in kW and time in hours
Converts between kWh and joules
Works out the cost of running an appliance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} runs a 2 kW heater for 3 hours and electricity costs 30p per kWh, can they work out how much it costs?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Electrical energy and power
topics.description: Calculate electrical power and energy transferred using P = IV, P = I²R and E = QV, and explain why power is transmitted at high voltage
evidence: Calculates power from current and potential difference
Calculates energy transferred by charge moving through a potential difference
Explains why high-voltage transmission reduces energy losses
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a kettle draws 10 A from a 230 V supply, can they work out its power?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Temperature versus thermal energy
topics.description: Distinguish temperature (average particle kinetic energy) from the total thermal energy of an object, which also depends on how much matter it contains and what it is made of
evidence: Explains why a bath of warm water can hold more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water
Uses the words temperature and thermal energy correctly
Predicts which sample needs more energy to warm by the same amount
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a cup of boiling water with a bath of warm water, can they explain which has more thermal energy and why that's different from which is hotter?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Specific heat capacity
topics.description: Explain specific heat capacity as the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, compare materials, and use it to explain why water heats and cools slowly and moderates coastal climates
evidence: Defines specific heat capacity with units J/kg°C
Explains why water needs more energy than the same mass of oil to warm by 1 °C
Links water's high specific heat capacity to coastal climates
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} notices sand on a beach is scorching while the sea is still cool, can they explain why using specific heat capacity?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Thermal equilibrium
topics.description: Explain that when objects at different temperatures are in contact in a closed system, energy transfers from hotter to colder until they reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium)
evidence: Predicts the direction of energy transfer between two objects
Predicts that the final temperature lies between the starting temperatures
Describes an investigation mixing hot and cold water
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} drops a hot metal spoon into a cold drink, can they describe what happens to the temperatures of both until they stop changing?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Calculating final temperature when mixing
topics.description: Use energy conservation (energy lost by the hot object = energy gained by the cold object) with Q = mcΔT to calculate the final temperature of a mixture or an unknown specific heat capacity
evidence: Sets up the equation energy lost = energy gained
Solves for the final temperature of mixed water
Explains why real results differ from calculated ones
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} mixes 200 g of water at 80 °C with 200 g of water at 20 °C, can they predict the final temperature and set up an equation that would work for unequal amounts?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Heat flows from hot to cold
topics.description: Explain that thermal energy spontaneously spreads from hotter to colder regions and becomes more evenly distributed (the second law of thermodynamics), and why this limits the efficiency of engines and power stations
evidence: States that heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never spontaneously the reverse
Explains that a fridge needs an energy input to move heat 'uphill'
Links energy spreading out to why no engine can be 100% efficient
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why an ice cube in a warm room never gets colder on its own, can they explain the rule about which way heat flows?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Cooling curves and rate of heat loss
topics.description: Interpret cooling curves — steep at first and levelling off as the object approaches room temperature — and explain how temperature difference, insulation thickness, material and surface area change the rate of heat loss
evidence: Explains why a hot drink cools fastest at first
Identifies factors that change the rate of heat transfer
Reads a cooling curve and describes how its steepness changes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records the temperature of a cup of tea every minute, can they explain why it cools quickly at first and more slowly later?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Designing to reduce heat transfer
topics.description: Design, test and improve a device that minimises or maximises thermal energy transfer (e.g. an insulated cup or a solar cooker), controlling variables and measuring temperature change
evidence: Chooses materials based on conduction, convection and radiation
Tests designs fairly by measuring temperature change over time
Evaluates results and suggests an improvement
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is challenged to keep an ice cube from melting for as long as possible, can they design a container and explain how each part reduces heat transfer?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Conduction explained by particles
topics.description: Explain conduction in solids as vibrating particles passing energy to neighbours, and why metals conduct so well (free electrons), while gases are poor conductors
evidence: Describes conduction as particle-to-particle energy transfer
Explains why metals are better conductors than plastics
Explains why trapped air is a good insulator
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} holds a metal spoon in hot soup, can they explain how the heat travels up the spoon to their hand?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Convection currents and density
topics.description: Explain convection currents as warmer fluid expanding, becoming less dense and rising while cooler, denser fluid sinks, and apply this to heaters, sea breezes and the atmosphere
evidence: Explains why warm air rises using density
Draws a convection current in a heated room or pan
Explains why convection cannot happen in solids
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a radiator under a window, can they draw how air moves around the room and explain why using density?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Infrared radiation and surfaces
topics.description: Explain that all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation, that hotter objects emit more, and that dark matt surfaces are better emitters and absorbers than light shiny ones
evidence: Ranks surfaces by how well they absorb and emit infrared
Explains why solar panels and radiators are often black
Explains why emergency blankets are shiny
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why marathon runners are wrapped in shiny foil blankets, can they explain how it keeps them warm?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Generating electricity by induction
topics.description: Explain that moving a magnet near a coil (or a coil in a magnetic field) induces a current, and that generators in power stations use this to transform kinetic energy into electrical energy
evidence: Describes how to induce a current with a magnet and coil
Lists ways to increase the induced current
Describes the energy transformation in a generator
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} moves a magnet in and out of a coil connected to a meter, can they explain why the needle flicks and how that relates to a power station?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Energy transformations in power stations
topics.description: Trace the energy chain in a thermal power station (fuel → thermal → kinetic in turbine → electrical) and in renewable alternatives, identifying where energy is dissipated
evidence: Describes each stage of a thermal power station
Compares the chain for wind, hydro and solar
Identifies the largest source of waste in a thermal power station
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how burning gas ends up lighting a lamp in their house, can they describe each energy transfer along the way?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Designing an energy-conversion device
topics.description: Design, build and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another within constraints (e.g. a solar oven, wind turbine or generator), measuring input and output to evaluate efficiency
evidence: Defines criteria and constraints for the device
Measures energy or power in and out
Refines the design based on test results
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a small wind turbine for a school project, can they explain how they would measure how well it works and decide what to improve?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Building an energy-accounting model
topics.description: Create a computational model (equations or a spreadsheet) that calculates the change in energy of one part of a system when the changes in the other parts and the flows in and out are known, and explain what each expression represents
evidence: Writes an energy balance equation for a system of two or three parts
Implements the calculation in a spreadsheet or short program
Explains the meaning of each term in the model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} models a roller coaster car with friction, can they set up a calculation that tracks kinetic, potential and dissipated energy at each point?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Comparing energy resources with data
topics.description: Use data on cost per kWh, reliability, land use and carbon emissions to compare energy resources and argue for an energy mix
evidence: Calculates and compares cost or emissions per kWh
Weighs reliability against environmental impact
Writes a justified recommendation for an energy mix
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given data on wind, gas and nuclear power, can they compare them on cost and carbon and argue for a sensible mix?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Letters as variables
topics.description: Understand that a letter in algebra stands for a number (often one that can vary), not for an object — so 3a means 3 × a, not '3 apples' — and that the same letter has the same value throughout an expression
evidence: Explains that a letter represents a number
Avoids the 'fruit salad' misconception (a = apples)
Recognises that a + a must be 2a, not a + b
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 'a + b = 10', can they explain that a and b stand for numbers — and give two different pairs of values that work?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Writing expressions from words
topics.description: Translate verbal descriptions into algebraic expressions, e.g. '5 more than twice a number' → 2n + 5, paying attention to order for subtraction and division
evidence: Writes expressions for phrases like 'three less than n' (n − 3)
Uses brackets when a whole quantity is multiplied
Describes an expression in words
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a cinema ticket costs £t and popcorn costs £4, can they write an expression for the cost of 3 tickets and one popcorn?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent expressions
topics.description: Recognise that two expressions are equivalent when they give the same value for every value of the variable, and test or prove equivalence by substitution and by simplifying
evidence: Identifies equivalent expressions such as 3(x + 2) and 3x + 6
Uses a counter-example to show two expressions are not equivalent
Explains why checking one value is not enough to prove equivalence
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown 2(x + 3) and 2x + 3, can they test some values and explain whether these always give the same answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Expanding brackets with negatives
topics.description: Expand and simplify expressions with negative terms and negative multipliers, such as −3(x − 4) and 5 − 2(x + 1), applying sign rules correctly
evidence: Expands −3(x − 4) to −3x + 12
Simplifies 5 − 2(x + 1) correctly
Explains a common sign error in expanding
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} expands 10 − 2(x − 3), can they get 16 − 2x and explain what happens to the −3?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Evaluating expressions with negative values
topics.description: Substitute negative numbers and fractions into expressions with powers and brackets, following the order of operations — e.g. knowing that for x = −3, x² = 9 but −x² = −9
evidence: Evaluates 2x² − 5x for x = −2
Distinguishes (−3)² from −3²
Uses brackets when substituting negatives on a calculator
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out x² − 4x when x = −1, can they get 5 and explain each step with the negative signs?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rewriting expressions to reveal meaning
topics.description: Rewrite expressions in different equivalent forms to show something useful about a situation, e.g. a + 0.05a = 1.05a shows that 'increase by 5%' is the same as 'multiply by 1.05'
evidence: Rewrites a percentage increase as a single multiplier
Explains what each form of an expression shows
Chooses the form that best answers a question
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that a price p rises by 20%, can they explain why p + 0.2p and 1.2p mean the same thing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Interpreting parts of an expression in context
topics.description: Interpret the terms, factors and coefficients of an expression in terms of the situation it models, and view complicated parts as single quantities — e.g. in P(1 + r)ⁿ, P is the starting amount and (1 + r) is the growth factor
evidence: Explains the meaning of each part of a formula in context
Identifies which part of an expression controls the rate of change
Treats a bracketed part as a single quantity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a taxi fare written as 3 + 1.5m, can they explain what the 3 and the 1.5 mean in real life?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Seeing structure in expressions
topics.description: Spot hidden structure in expressions to rewrite them — e.g. seeing x⁴ − y⁴ as (x²)² − (y²)², or 4x² + 12x + 9 as (2x + 3)² — choosing a form that makes the problem easier
evidence: Recognises a difference of two squares in disguise
Recognises a perfect-square trinomial
Uses substitution (let u = x²) to see a quadratic in disguise
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to factorise x⁴ − 16, can they spot it as a difference of two squares — twice?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Solving x² = p and x³ = p
topics.description: Use square-root and cube-root symbols to solve equations of the form x² = p and x³ = p, recognising that x² = p has two solutions and that √2 is irrational
evidence: Solves x² = 49 giving both ±7
Solves x³ = −8
Estimates √20 between two whole numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} solves x² = 36, can they explain why there are two answers?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Approximating irrational numbers
topics.description: Locate irrational numbers such as √2, √50 and π on a number line by finding rational approximations, and compare their sizes
evidence: Places √2 between 1.4 and 1.5 on a number line
Orders a list containing integers, fractions and roots
Explains why √2 cannot be written as a fraction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether √50 is closer to 7 or 8, can they explain how they know without a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Laws of exponents
topics.description: Apply the laws of exponents for multiplying, dividing and raising powers to powers — aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ — with numbers and variables
evidence: Simplifies x³ × x⁴ and y⁸ ÷ y²
Simplifies (2x³)²
Explains a law by writing out the repeated multiplication
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to simplify x³ × x⁵, can they explain why the answer is x⁸ and not x¹⁵?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Zero and negative exponents
topics.description: Explain why a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ using patterns and the laws of exponents, and evaluate expressions such as 2⁻³ and 10⁻²
evidence: Uses a halving pattern to explain 2⁰ = 1
Evaluates negative powers as fractions
Simplifies expressions mixing positive and negative exponents
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 10⁻², can they explain why that equals 0.01 by continuing the pattern 10², 10¹, 10⁰…?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating with scientific notation
topics.description: Multiply, divide, add and subtract numbers in scientific notation, choose sensible units, and interpret calculator output such as 3.2E-5
evidence: Multiplies (3 × 10⁴)(2 × 10⁵) using exponent laws
Divides numbers in scientific notation
Interprets 'E' notation on a calculator
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to find how far light travels in a year (3 × 10⁸ m/s × 3.2 × 10⁷ s), can they do the calculation in scientific notation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractional exponents and radicals
topics.description: Explain fractional exponents by extending the exponent laws — a^(1/n) is the nth root of a and a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ — and rewrite expressions between radical and exponent form
evidence: Evaluates 8^(2/3) and 16^(−1/2)
Rewrites √x³ as x^(3/2)
Explains why 5^(1/2) must equal √5 using exponent laws
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 27^(1/3), can they explain why it means the cube root of 27?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simplifying surds
topics.description: Simplify and calculate with surds, e.g. √12 = 2√3, √2 × √8 = 4, and rationalise simple denominators
evidence: Simplifies √48 using square factors
