topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a satellite moves to twice its distance from Earth's centre, can they predict how the gravitational force changes?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Coulomb's law
topics.description: Use Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂/r² to describe and predict the electrostatic force between two charged objects, comparing its form with gravitation
evidence: Calculates the force between two charges
Predicts attraction or repulsion from the signs
Compares the structure of Coulomb's law with gravitation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} halves the distance between two charged balloons, can they predict how the force between them changes?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Fields and forces at a distance
topics.description: Explain non-contact forces using fields — gravitational, electric and magnetic — drawing field-line diagrams and describing field strength and direction
evidence: Draws field lines around a magnet, a charge and a planet
Explains what closer field lines mean
Explains how a field transfers a force without contact
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees iron filings around a bar magnet, can they explain what the pattern tells them about the magnetic field?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Magnetic field patterns of wires and solenoids
topics.description: Map and draw the magnetic field patterns produced by a current in a straight wire (concentric circles) and in a solenoid (like a bar magnet), use the right-hand grip rule to find field direction, and plan an investigation showing that reversing the current reverses the field
evidence: Describes the field pattern around a straight wire
Explains how a solenoid's field is strengthened
Uses the right-hand grip rule to find field direction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} places a compass next to a wire and switches on the current, can they explain why the needle moves?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Force–extension graphs and spring constant
topics.description: Investigate Hooke's law (F = ke), plot force–extension graphs, find the spring constant from the gradient and identify the limit of proportionality
evidence: Plots force against extension
Calculates the spring constant from the gradient
Identifies where the graph stops being linear
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hangs weights on a spring and records its extension, can they find the spring constant from a graph?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Calculating pressure in liquids (p = ρgh)
topics.description: Explain that pressure in a liquid increases with depth and density (p = ρgh), and use it to explain dams, diving and upthrust
evidence: Calculates pressure at a given depth
Explains why dams are thicker at the bottom
Explains upthrust as a pressure difference
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} dives to the bottom of a swimming pool and feels their ears hurt, can they explain why pressure is greater there?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Stopping distances
topics.description: Explain stopping distance as thinking distance plus braking distance, and how speed, reaction time, road conditions and vehicle condition affect each
evidence: Distinguishes thinking and braking distance
Lists factors affecting each
Explains why braking distance increases more than speed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a driver is tired and the road is wet, can they explain which part of the stopping distance each one affects?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Waves transfer energy, not matter
topics.description: Explain that a wave transfers energy (and information) from one place to another while the particles of the medium only oscillate about fixed positions, using evidence such as a floating cork bobbing on ripples
evidence: Explains why a cork on a pond moves up and down but not along with the ripples
Distinguishes the motion of the wave from the motion of the medium
Identifies the energy carried by everyday waves (sound, light, water)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a duck bobbing as ripples pass, can they explain why the duck isn't carried across the pond?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Amplitude and the energy of a wave
topics.description: Describe how the energy carried by a wave increases with its amplitude, linking louder sounds and brighter light to larger amplitudes
evidence: States that larger amplitude means more energy carried
Links loudness of a sound to amplitude
Compares two wave diagrams and says which carries more energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown two waves with the same wavelength but different heights, can they say which carries more energy and why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reading wave diagrams and graphs
topics.description: Read amplitude and wavelength from a displacement–distance graph and amplitude and period from a displacement–time graph, and explain what each axis shows
evidence: Measures amplitude and wavelength from a displacement–distance graph
Reads the time period from a displacement–time graph
Explains why the two graphs look alike but show different things
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a displacement–time graph of a wave, can they read off its amplitude and its period, with units?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Frequency and period (f = 1/T)
topics.description: Define frequency as the number of waves passing a point per second (hertz) and time period as the time for one wave, and convert between them using f = 1/T
evidence: Calculates the frequency of a wave with a period of 0.02 s
Calculates the period of a 440 Hz sound
Explains what 1 Hz means
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a wave has a period of 0.25 s, can they work out its frequency and explain what that number means?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Calculating wave speed (v = fλ)
topics.description: Use the wave equation v = f × λ to calculate wave speed, frequency or wavelength, rearranging as needed and using correct units
evidence: Calculates the speed of a wave from its frequency and wavelength
Rearranges to find wavelength from speed and frequency
Converts kHz and cm into Hz and m before calculating
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a sound wave has a frequency of 680 Hz and travels at 340 m/s, can they find its wavelength?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Measuring the speed of sound and water waves
topics.description: Plan and carry out methods to measure wave speed — timing an echo or using two microphones for sound, and measuring frequency and wavelength in a ripple tank — and evaluate sources of error
evidence: Describes a method to measure the speed of sound in air
Measures wavelength in a ripple tank using a strobe or photo and a ruler
Suggests how to reduce timing errors
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has two microphones and a timer, can they describe how to measure the speed of sound and what would make the result unreliable?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Wave speed depends on the medium
topics.description: Explain that a wave's speed depends on the medium it travels through — sound is fastest in solids and cannot cross a vacuum, light is slower in glass than in air — and that at a boundary the frequency stays the same while the wavelength changes
evidence: Orders the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases
Explains why sound cannot travel through space but light can
Predicts that wavelength shortens when a wave slows down at a boundary
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, can they say what happens to its wavelength when it passes from air into water?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Compressions and rarefactions
topics.description: Describe a longitudinal wave in terms of compressions and rarefactions of the medium, identify the wavelength on a longitudinal diagram, and model it with a slinky
evidence: Labels compressions and rarefactions on a diagram
Marks one wavelength on a longitudinal wave
Uses a slinky to show particles moving parallel to the energy transfer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pushes and pulls one end of a slinky, can they point to a compression and a rarefaction and show one wavelength?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Hearing range, ultrasound and infrasound
topics.description: State that humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, define ultrasound and infrasound by frequency, and compare hearing ranges of animals and of people as they age
evidence: States the approximate human hearing range in Hz
Classifies frequencies as infrasound, audible or ultrasound
Explains why a dog whistle is silent to people
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a bat calls at 50 000 Hz, can they explain why people cannot hear it?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Sound waves on an oscilloscope
topics.description: Interpret oscilloscope or microphone traces of sounds — taller traces are louder, more closely packed traces are higher pitched — and calculate frequency from the time base
evidence: Compares two traces for loudness and pitch
Calculates frequency from squares per wave and the time-base setting
Sketches the trace for a quieter, higher note
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees two oscilloscope traces of notes, can they say which is louder, which is higher, and estimate one frequency from the time base?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Echoes and echo-sounding calculations
topics.description: Use echoes to measure distances with distance = speed × time ÷ 2, as in sonar and echo-sounding, explaining why the time is halved
evidence: Calculates the depth of the sea from a sonar echo time
Explains why the time is divided by two
Describes how bats or ships use echoes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears an echo from a cliff 2 s after shouting, can they work out how far away the cliff is if sound travels at 340 m/s?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Ultrasound imaging and detection
topics.description: Explain how pulses of ultrasound are partly reflected at each boundary between materials, and how timing the echoes builds an image in prenatal scans, finds cracks in metal (non-destructive testing) and maps the sea bed
evidence: Explains why ultrasound is partly reflected at each tissue boundary
Calculates the depth of a boundary from an echo time
Explains why ultrasound is safer than X-rays for prenatal scans
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an ultrasound scan of a baby, can they explain how echoes from different tissues make the picture?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Sound level and the decibel scale
topics.description: Interpret the decibel scale as logarithmic — each increase of 10 dB is ten times the intensity — and use it to judge risks of hearing damage
evidence: Explains why 80 dB is 100 times the intensity of 60 dB
Places everyday sounds on the decibel scale
Explains why prolonged exposure above about 85 dB is risky
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a concert is 110 dB and a busy street is 80 dB, can they say how many times more intense the concert is?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Natural frequency and resonance
topics.description: Explain that objects have natural frequencies and that driving them at that frequency produces large-amplitude oscillations (resonance), with examples such as instruments, glasses and bridges
evidence: Defines natural frequency
Explains why pushing a swing in time builds up amplitude
Gives a useful and a harmful example of resonance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a singer break a glass with a note, can they explain why only one particular pitch works?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Superposition and interference
topics.description: Explain that when waves meet their displacements add (superposition), producing constructive and destructive interference, and that the waves pass through each other unchanged
evidence: Adds two wave pulses on a diagram
Explains how noise-cancelling headphones work
Describes where loud and quiet spots appear between two speakers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} walks between two speakers playing the same note, can they explain why the sound gets louder and quieter in different places?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Standing waves and harmonics
topics.description: Explain standing waves on a string or in a pipe as the superposition of two waves travelling in opposite directions, identify nodes and antinodes, and relate harmonics to the notes of instruments
evidence: Labels nodes and antinodes on a standing wave
Finds the wavelength of the first harmonic of a string of known length
Explains why shortening a guitar string raises the pitch
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} presses a guitar string halfway along, can they explain why the note goes up an octave?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Diffraction
topics.description: Describe diffraction as the spreading of waves through gaps and around obstacles, greatest when the gap is similar to the wavelength, and use it to explain why sound bends round doorways but light does not noticeably
evidence: Sketches wavefronts passing through narrow and wide gaps
States the condition for maximum diffraction
Explains why you can hear but not see round a corner
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} can hear someone talking in the next room but can't see them, can they use wavelengths to explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Polarisation
topics.description: Explain that transverse waves can be polarised to oscillate in one plane, that longitudinal waves cannot, and use this as evidence that light is transverse; describe uses such as polarising sunglasses
evidence: Explains why only transverse waves can be polarised
Describes what happens when two polarising filters are rotated
Explains how polarising sunglasses reduce glare
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks through two polarising filters and rotates one, can they explain why the view goes dark?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Specular and diffuse reflection
topics.description: Distinguish specular reflection from smooth surfaces (which forms images) from diffuse reflection from rough surfaces (which scatters light), applying the law of reflection at each point
evidence: Draws rays reflecting from a smooth and a rough surface
Explains why paper reflects light but does not form an image
Uses the law of reflection on an uneven surface
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a mirror and a sheet of white paper, can they explain why only one shows their reflection even though both reflect light?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Explaining refraction with wavefronts
topics.description: Explain refraction as a change in speed at a boundary that makes wavefronts change direction, bending towards the normal when the wave slows down, with no change of direction along the normal
evidence: Draws wavefronts bending as they enter a slower medium
Predicts which way light bends entering and leaving a glass block
Explains why there is no bending at 90° to the surface
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} shines a ray into a glass block at an angle, can they explain with wavefronts why it bends towards the normal?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Refractive index and Snell's law
topics.description: Use refractive index n = c/v and Snell's law n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ to calculate angles of refraction and speeds of light in materials
evidence: Calculates the speed of light in glass from its refractive index
Finds an angle of refraction using Snell's law
Measures n for a glass block from ray data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures a ray entering glass at 40° and leaving the surface at 25°, can they calculate the refractive index?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Total internal reflection and optical fibres
topics.description: Explain total internal reflection when light in a denser medium meets a boundary at more than the critical angle, and apply it to optical fibres and endoscopes
evidence: States both conditions for total internal reflection
Draws the path of light along an optical fibre
Explains why fibres carry signals with little loss
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees light trapped inside a curved glass fibre, can they explain why it doesn't escape through the sides?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Converging and diverging lenses
topics.description: Describe how converging (convex) and diverging (concave) lenses refract parallel rays, define principal focus and focal length, and use lens symbols in diagrams
evidence: Draws parallel rays passing through each type of lens
Marks the principal focus and focal length
Explains why a diverging lens has a virtual focus
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} holds a magnifying glass in sunlight, can they explain where the bright spot forms and what that distance is called?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Magnification
topics.description: Calculate magnification as image height ÷ object height (a ratio with no units), and relate it to the ray diagram
evidence: Calculates magnification from two heights
Explains why magnification has no unit
Finds an image height from the magnification
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures a 2 cm object producing a 7 cm image, can they find the magnification and explain what it means?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The thin lens equation

Calculates the power of a lens in dioptres
Checks an answer against a scale ray diagram
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a lens of focal length 10 cm and an object 15 cm away, can they calculate where the image forms?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The eye, cameras and correcting vision
topics.description: Describe the eye and the camera as converging-lens systems that form real images, and explain how short and long sight are corrected with diverging and converging lenses
evidence: Labels the parts of the eye that focus light
Explains short sight and its correction with a ray diagram
Compares the eye with a camera
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a friend can't read distant signs, can they explain what is going wrong in the eye and which lens fixes it?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Shared properties of electromagnetic waves
topics.description: State that all electromagnetic waves are transverse, travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, need no medium and transfer energy, differing only in wavelength and frequency
evidence: Lists the properties all EM waves share
Explains how light from the Sun reaches Earth
Orders EM waves by frequency and wavelength
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how radio waves and X-rays are alike, can they list what all electromagnetic waves have in common?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Calculating with electromagnetic waves
topics.description: Use v = fλ with the speed of light to calculate frequencies and wavelengths across the spectrum, working in standard form
evidence: Calculates the wavelength of a 100 MHz radio wave
Finds the frequency of green light from its wavelength
Uses prefixes such as nano- and mega- correctly
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a radio station broadcasts at 98 MHz, can they calculate the wavelength?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Uses of the electromagnetic spectrum
topics.description: Explain why each region of the spectrum suits its uses — radio for broadcasting, microwaves for satellites and cooking, infrared for heating and remote controls, visible light in fibres, UV for sterilising, X-rays and gamma for imaging and treatment
evidence: Matches each region to a use
Explains a use in terms of a property such as penetration or absorption
Explains why microwaves heat food
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why X-rays are used for broken bones, can they explain using what X-rays do to bone and to soft tissue?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Ionising and non-ionising radiation risks
topics.description: Explain that higher-frequency EM radiation carries more energy, that UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can damage cells, and that lower-frequency radiation mainly causes heating
evidence: Separates ionising from non-ionising radiation
Explains why UV can cause skin cancer
Describes how radiographers limit exposure
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why sunscreen blocks UV but nobody worries about radio waves, can they explain the difference?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Evaluating claims about electromagnetic radiation
topics.description: Evaluate claims in media about health effects of EM radiation (mobile phones, Wi-Fi, sunbeds, X-rays), checking frequency, energy, dose, sources and evidence quality
evidence: Identifies the frequency band a claim is about
Judges whether the evidence shows correlation or causation
Checks a source for bias and data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a post claiming Wi-Fi causes cancer, can they judge the claim using what they know about frequency and evidence?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Producing and receiving radio waves
topics.description: Explain that oscillating charges in an aerial (driven by an alternating current) emit radio waves, and that absorbed radio waves induce an alternating current of the same frequency in a receiving aerial
evidence: Explains how an alternating current produces radio waves
Explains how a receiver aerial produces a signal
Links the frequency of the current to the frequency of the wave
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how a radio picks up a station, can they explain what the radio wave does to electrons in the aerial?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Emission, absorption and temperature
topics.description: Explain that all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation, that hotter objects emit more and at shorter wavelengths, and that an object's temperature stays constant when it absorbs and emits at the same rate, applying this to Earth's temperature
evidence: Explains why a heated metal glows red then white
Explains constant temperature as balanced emission and absorption
Links the balance to Earth's average temperature
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a stove ring heating up, can they explain why its colour changes and what happens when its temperature stops rising?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Wave and particle models of light
topics.description: Evaluate evidence that light behaves as a wave (diffraction, interference) and as particles called photons (photoelectric effect), and explain why scientists use whichever model fits a situation
evidence: Gives evidence for the wave model
Describes the photoelectric effect qualitatively
Explains why two models are kept rather than one
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that, for some metals, dim blue light can knock electrons out but very bright red light can't, can they explain why this supports a particle model?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Photon energy (E = hf)
topics.description: Calculate photon energy with E = hf and E = hc/λ, and use it to explain why higher-frequency radiation is more damaging
evidence: Calculates the energy of a photon of given frequency
Compares photon energies for UV and infrared
Explains why photon energy, not brightness, decides ionisation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a UV photon and an infrared photon, can they calculate which carries more energy and by how much?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Analog and digital signals
topics.description: Distinguish analog signals, which vary continuously, from digital signals, which take only a few discrete values (often 0 and 1), using examples such as vinyl records and streamed music
evidence: Sketches an analog and a digital signal
Classifies everyday signals as analog or digital
Explains what 'discrete values' means
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a vinyl record and a music file, can they explain how the sound is stored differently?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Why digital signals are more reliable
topics.description: Explain that noise added during transmission can be removed from digital signals by regenerating clean pulses, whereas noise in analog signals is amplified with the signal
evidence: Shows on a sketch how noise affects each type of signal
Explains regeneration of digital pulses
Gives an advantage of digital broadcasting
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears crackle on an old analog radio but not on digital radio, can they explain the difference?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Sampling and bit depth
topics.description: Describe how an analog signal is digitised by sampling at regular intervals and storing each sample as a binary number, and calculate how sample rate and bits per sample affect quality and file size
evidence: Digitises a simple waveform at a given sample rate
Calculates the number of values available from n bits
Estimates file size from sample rate, bit depth and duration
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records 10 s of audio at 44 100 samples per second with 16 bits each, can they estimate the file size?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Pros and cons of digital storage and transmission
topics.description: Evaluate the advantages of digital information (reliable storage, easy copying and sharing, compression) against drawbacks such as easy deletion, security risks and theft
evidence: Lists advantages of digital storage
Explains a security risk of digital information
Argues a position about storing family photos digitally
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is deciding whether to keep only digital copies of family photos, can they weigh up the advantages and risks?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Carrying information with waves
topics.description: Explain how communication systems choose wave types to carry information — radio and microwaves for wireless and satellite links, light in optical fibres — and how signals are encoded on a carrier wave
evidence: Explains why satellites use microwaves
Compares copper cable, optical fibre and wireless links
Describes encoding a signal on a carrier wave
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why internet cables under the sea use optical fibre, can they explain the advantages?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: The Doppler effect
topics.description: Explain that a moving source produces waves bunched up ahead (higher frequency) and stretched out behind (lower frequency), with examples from sirens and astronomy
evidence: Draws wavefronts from a moving source
Explains the change in pitch of a passing siren
Predicts the shift for a source moving away
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears an ambulance siren drop in pitch as it passes, can they explain with a wavefront drawing what's happening?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Red-shift and the expanding universe
topics.description: Explain that light from distant galaxies is shifted to longer wavelengths, that more distant galaxies show greater red-shift, and how this supports the Big Bang model
evidence: Explains what red-shift means for spectral lines
Describes the link between distance and red-shift
Explains how red-shift supports an expanding universe
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that a galaxy's spectral lines are shifted towards red, can they explain what it tells us about the galaxy's motion?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Intensity falls with distance
topics.description: Explain that the intensity of light or sound from a point source falls with the inverse square of distance because the energy spreads over a larger area
evidence: Explains why doubling distance quarters intensity
Calculates intensity at a new distance
Links the law to the area of a sphere
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} moves twice as far from a lamp, can they predict how bright it will appear and explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Charging by electron transfer
topics.description: Explain charging by friction as the transfer of electrons from one material to another, so one object becomes negative and the other equally positive, with total charge conserved
evidence: Explains which object gains electrons when a balloon is rubbed on hair
States that positive charge is not transferred
Explains why the two objects end up with equal and opposite charges
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} rubs a balloon on a jumper and it becomes negative, can they explain what happened to the jumper and why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Electric fields
topics.description: Describe the electric field around a charged object, draw field lines for isolated charges, and explain that a charge in the field feels a force that is stronger closer to the object, causing sparks when the field is strong enough
evidence: Draws field lines around a positive and a negative charge
Explains the direction of force on a charge in a field
Explains why sparks jump from strongly charged objects
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} brings a small charged ball near a charged dome, can they describe the field and predict the force on the ball?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Uses and dangers of static electricity
topics.description: Explain dangers of static (sparks when refuelling, shocks) and how earthing prevents them, and describe uses such as electrostatic spray painting, photocopiers and smoke precipitators
evidence: Explains why fuel tankers are earthed
Describes how electrostatic spray painting gives an even coat
Explains what earthing does to excess charge
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a fuel tanker connected by a wire to the ground before refuelling, can they explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Current as rate of flow of charge (Q = It)
topics.description: Define current as the rate of flow of charge and use Q = I × t to calculate charge in coulombs, current in amperes or time
evidence: Calculates charge passing in a given time
Rearranges Q = It to find current
Converts minutes to seconds before calculating
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows 2 A flows through a lamp for 5 minutes, can they calculate how much charge has passed?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Conventional current and electron flow
topics.description: Explain that conventional current is shown flowing from positive to negative while electrons actually drift from negative to positive, and why the convention persists
evidence: Marks conventional current on a circuit diagram
Marks the direction of electron flow
Explains why the two directions differ
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an arrow showing current leaving the positive terminal, can they explain which way the electrons are moving?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Potential difference as energy per charge
topics.description: Define potential difference as the energy transferred per unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C) and use V = E/Q
evidence: Explains what 12 V means in joules and coulombs
Calculates energy transferred by a charge moving through a pd
Distinguishes pd across a component from current through it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a battery is 9 V, can they explain what that means for each coulomb of charge?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Using ammeters and voltmeters
topics.description: Connect ammeters in series and voltmeters in parallel, read analogue and digital meters with suitable ranges, and check for zero errors
evidence: Draws a circuit with an ammeter and a voltmeter correctly placed
Reads an analogue meter scale
Explains why a voltmeter goes in parallel
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to measure the current through and voltage across a lamp, can they draw where each meter goes and explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Symbols for secondary circuit components
topics.description: Recognise and draw symbols for resistors, variable resistors, diodes, LEDs, LDRs, thermistors, fuses, ammeters and voltmeters, and build circuits from diagrams
evidence: Draws the symbols for an LDR and a thermistor
Builds a circuit correctly from a diagram
Identifies the components in an unfamiliar diagram
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a circuit diagram with a thermistor and an LED, can they name every component and build it?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: What affects the resistance of a wire
topics.description: Investigate how a wire's length, thickness, material and temperature affect its resistance, controlling variables and plotting resistance against length
evidence: Predicts how doubling length changes resistance
Plans a fair test of resistance against length
Explains why thicker wires have lower resistance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the resistance of 20 cm, 40 cm and 60 cm of the same wire, can they predict the pattern and explain it?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Resistance explained by electrons and ions
topics.description: Explain resistance in metals as electrons colliding with vibrating metal ions, and use this to explain why resistance rises with temperature and why current heats a wire
evidence: Describes electrons colliding with lattice ions
Explains why a filament's resistance rises as it heats
Links collisions to the heating effect of a current
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a bulb filament's resistance increase as it glows, can they explain why using particles?

topics.subject: Science

evidence: Describes how the angle of the plane gives each conic
Matches standard equations to the four conics
Identifies conics in real objects and images
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a torch beam hitting a wall at different angles, can they name the conic formed each time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The parabola from focus and directrix
topics.description: Derive the equation of a parabola as the locus of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix, for example y² = 4ax from the focus (a, 0) and the directrix x = −a, or y = x²/(4p) from (0, p) and y = −p
evidence: Writes the distances to the focus and directrix algebraically
Derives y² = 4ax by squaring and simplifying
Finds the equation from a given focus and directrix
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given the focus (0, 2) and the directrix y = −2, can they derive the equation of the parabola?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Features of the parabola y² = 4ax
topics.description: Identify the vertex, focus, directrix and axis of parabolas such as y² = 4ax, x² = 4ay and translated forms (y − k)² = 4a(x − h)
evidence: States the focus and directrix of y² = 12x
Finds the vertex and focus of (y − 1)² = 8(x + 2)
Sketches a parabola opening to the left
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given (y + 3)² = −8(x − 1), can they find the vertex, focus and directrix and sketch the curve?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The ellipse
topics.description: Sketch the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, identify its intercepts and major and minor axes, and see it as a circle stretched in one direction
evidence: Sketches an ellipse from its equation
States the lengths of the major and minor axes
Explains the ellipse as a stretched circle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, can they sketch the ellipse and mark its intercepts?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Foci of an ellipse
topics.description: Use the fact that the sum of the distances from any point on an ellipse to the two foci is constant (2a) to derive its equation, and locate the foci using b² = a² − c²
evidence: Finds the foci of x²/25 + y²/16 = 1
Derives the equation of an ellipse from its foci
Explains how to draw an ellipse with string and two pins
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told the foci of an ellipse are (±4, 0) and the sum of distances is 10, can they find its equation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The hyperbola
topics.description: Sketch the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 with its two branches, vertices and asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x
evidence: Sketches a hyperbola from its equation
Finds the equations of the asymptotes
Explains why there are no points with |x| < a
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given x²/16 − y²/9 = 1, can they sketch the hyperbola with its asymptotes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Foci of a hyperbola
topics.description: Use the fact that the difference of the distances from any point on a hyperbola to the two foci is constant (2a) to derive its equation, and locate the foci using b² = c² − a²
evidence: Finds the foci of x²/9 − y²/16 = 1
Derives the equation of a hyperbola from its foci
Contrasts the hyperbola's focal property with the ellipse's
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told the foci of a hyperbola are (±5, 0) and the difference of distances is 6, can they find its equation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The rectangular hyperbola xy = c²
topics.description: Recognise xy = c² as a hyperbola with perpendicular asymptotes (the coordinate axes), use the parametric form (ct, c/t), and link it to y = k/x
evidence: Sketches xy = 16 and states its asymptotes
Writes the parametric form of a rectangular hyperbola
Explains the link with inverse proportion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given xy = 9, can they explain why it is a hyperbola and give a parametric form?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Eccentricity and the focus–directrix definition
topics.description: Define every conic as the locus where the distance to a focus is e times the distance to a directrix, with e < 1 for an ellipse, e = 1 for a parabola and e > 1 for a hyperbola, and find foci and directrices x = ±a/e
evidence: Calculates the eccentricity of an ellipse and a hyperbola
Finds the directrices from a and e
Explains how the shape changes as e varies
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given the ellipse x²/25 + y²/16 = 1, can they find its eccentricity, foci and directrices?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Parametric equations of conics
topics.description: Use parametric forms of the conics: (at², 2at) for y² = 4ax, (a cos θ, b sin θ) for an ellipse, (a cosh t, b sinh t) or (a sec θ, b tan θ) for a hyperbola, and (ct, c/t) for xy = c²
evidence: Verifies that a parametric point satisfies the Cartesian equation
Converts each parametric form to Cartesian form
Chooses a convenient parameter for a problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given x = 3 cos θ, y = 2 sin θ, can they show the curve is an ellipse and find its Cartesian equation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tangents and normals to conics
topics.description: Find equations of tangents and normals to conics using implicit or parametric differentiation, including standard results such as the tangent ty = x + at² to y² = 4ax
evidence: Finds the tangent to an ellipse at a given point
Derives the tangent to y² = 4ax at (at², 2at)
Finds where a normal meets the curve again
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given the point (2 cos θ, sin θ) on an ellipse, can they find the equation of the tangent there?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Intersections of lines and conics
topics.description: Find where a line meets a conic by substitution, and use the discriminant to find conditions for a line to be a tangent, such as c = a/m for y = mx + c and y² = 4ax
evidence: Finds the intersections of a line and an ellipse
Uses the discriminant to show a line is a tangent
Finds the values of m for which a line through a point is a tangent
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has the line y = mx + 2 and the ellipse x² + 4y² = 8, can they find the values of m for which the line is a tangent?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Focal chords of a parabola
topics.description: Use the parametric form to show that the endpoints of a focal chord of y² = 4ax have parameters with pq = −1, and find the length of the latus rectum (4a)
evidence: Shows that pq = −1 for a focal chord
Finds the length of the latus rectum
Finds the other end of a focal chord
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows one end of a focal chord of y² = 8x is at (2, 4), can they find the other end?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Locus problems with conics
topics.description: Find the locus of a point defined using a conic, such as the midpoint of a chord or the intersection of two tangents, by writing it in terms of a parameter and eliminating the parameter
evidence: Finds the locus of midpoints of chords of a parabola
Finds where two tangents meet in terms of parameters
Eliminates the parameter to find a Cartesian locus
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} considers the midpoints of all chords of y² = 4x through the origin, can they find the locus of the midpoints?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Recognising conics from their equations
topics.description: Identify a conic from an equation such as 4x² + 9y² − 16x + 18y = 11 by completing the square, and find its centre, axes and foci
evidence: Completes the square in x and y
Writes the equation in standard form
Finds the centre and foci of the translated conic
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given 9x² − 4y² − 36x − 8y = 4, can they identify the conic and find its centre?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Transforming conics
topics.description: Apply translations, stretches, reflections and rotations through 90° to conics and find the transformed equations, including using matrices
evidence: Finds the equation after a translation by a vector
Finds the image of an ellipse under a stretch
Uses a matrix to transform a conic
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} translates y² = 8x by the vector (3, −1), can they write the new equation and state the new focus?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Conics in polar form
topics.description: Use the polar equation r = l/(1 + e cos θ), with a focus at the pole, to describe ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas, and relate l and e to the shape
evidence: Identifies the conic from a polar equation
Converts r = 6/(2 + cos θ) to Cartesian form
Finds the nearest and furthest distances from the focus
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given r = 8/(1 + 0.5 cos θ), can they identify the conic and find its closest distance to the pole?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reflective properties of conics
topics.description: Explain the reflective properties of conics: rays parallel to the axis of a parabola reflect through the focus, and rays from one focus of an ellipse reflect through the other
evidence: Explains why a satellite dish is parabolic
Explains the whispering-gallery effect in an elliptical room
Justifies a reflective property using a tangent
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why a car headlight has a parabolic mirror with the bulb at the focus, can they explain?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Conics in orbits and engineering
topics.description: Use conics to model real situations: planetary orbits as ellipses with the Sun at a focus, comet paths, reflectors and hyperbolic navigation, judging which conic and parameters fit
evidence: Describes a planetary orbit using eccentricity
Finds the closest and furthest distances of an orbit
Explains why a parabolic or hyperbolic path means an object does not return
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given the eccentricity and major axis of Earth's orbit, can they find its closest and furthest distances from the Sun?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of an ellipse
topics.description: Show that an ellipse with semi-axes a and b has area πab, by parametric integration or by stretching a circle
evidence: Sets up a parametric integral for the area of an ellipse
Evaluates the integral using a double-angle identity
Explains the result as a stretch of a circle of area πa²
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given x²/16 + y²/9 = 1, can they find the area of the ellipse and justify the formula?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Intermolecular forces and hydrogen bonding
topics.description: Distinguish London (induced dipole) forces, permanent dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds between N–H, O–H or F–H groups and lone pairs, and use them to explain trends in boiling point and solubility
evidence: Identifies the strongest intermolecular force in a substance
Explains why water and alcohols have high boiling points
Draws a hydrogen bond between two molecules with lone pairs and partial charges
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) with propane (−42 °C), which have similar masses, can they explain the difference?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Aldehydes, ketones and the carbonyl group
topics.description: Recognise the polar C=O carbonyl group, with a δ+ carbon and δ− oxygen, in aldehydes (–CHO at the end of a chain) and ketones (C=O within the chain), and name them with -al and -one
evidence: Distinguishes aldehydes from ketones by structure
Names propanal and butanone
Explains why the carbonyl carbon is δ+
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown the structures of propanal and propanone, can they name each and explain how they differ?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Physical properties of aldehydes and ketones
topics.description: Explain that aldehydes and ketones have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass (permanent dipoles) but lower than alcohols (no hydrogen bonds between molecules), and that small ones dissolve in water by hydrogen bonding to it
evidence: Orders an alkane, aldehyde and alcohol of similar Mr by boiling point
Explains why propanone mixes with water
Explains why longer-chain aldehydes are less soluble
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given butane, propanal and propan-1-ol, can they put them in order of boiling point and explain the order?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Distillation versus reflux in alcohol oxidation
topics.description: Explain why oxidising a primary alcohol with acidified dichromate and distilling off the product as it forms gives an aldehyde, while heating under reflux gives a carboxylic acid, and draw both set-ups
evidence: Draws apparatus for distillation and for reflux
Explains why the aldehyde distils off before it is oxidised further
Chooses conditions to make propanal or propanoic acid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to make ethanal rather than ethanoic acid from ethanol, can they explain which apparatus to use and why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Tollens' and Fehling's tests for aldehydes
topics.description: Use Tollens' reagent (a silver mirror forms) and Fehling's or Benedict's solution (blue to brick-red precipitate) to distinguish aldehydes, which are easily oxidised, from ketones, which are not
evidence: States the positive results for both tests
Explains the tests in terms of oxidation of the aldehyde
Identifies which reagent is reduced
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has two unlabelled colourless liquids, propanal and propanone, can they choose a test to tell them apart and predict the results?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Detecting carbonyl compounds with 2,4-DNP
topics.description: Use 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent), which gives a yellow-orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones, and identify the compound from the melting point of the purified derivative
evidence: States the positive result with 2,4-DNP
Explains why the test does not tell aldehydes from ketones
Uses a melting point to identify a recrystallised derivative
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNP, can they explain what this shows and how to identify the exact compound?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Nucleophiles
topics.description: Explain that a nucleophile is an electron-pair donor that attacks a δ+ atom, identify nucleophiles such as OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃ and the hydride ion from NaBH₄, and contrast them with electrophiles
evidence: Defines a nucleophile
Identifies the lone pair or negative charge used by a nucleophile
Contrasts nucleophiles and electrophiles with examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given OH⁻, NO₂⁺, NH₃ and Br₂, can they sort them into nucleophiles and electrophiles and explain why?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyl compounds
topics.description: Draw the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to C=O: the nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon, the π electrons move onto oxygen, and the intermediate is protonated
evidence: Draws curly arrows for each step
Explains why the carbon is attacked
Contrasts nucleophilic addition with electrophilic addition to C=C
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given propanal and the CN⁻ ion, can they draw the mechanism of the reaction?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reducing aldehydes and ketones
topics.description: Reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols with NaBH₄, writing equations with [H], and recognise this as the reverse of oxidation
evidence: Writes the equation for the reduction of propanone using [H]
Predicts the alcohol from a given carbonyl compound
Explains the reaction as nucleophilic addition of a hydride ion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reduces butanal and butanone with NaBH₄, can they name both products and classify them?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Adding cyanide: hydroxynitriles
topics.description: Describe the reaction of aldehydes and ketones with KCN followed by dilute acid to form hydroxynitriles, explain the mechanism, and recognise it as a way to add a carbon atom to a chain
evidence: Writes the equation and names the hydroxynitrile
Explains why KCN is used rather than HCN gas
Explains why this lengthens the carbon chain
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reacts ethanal with KCN and acid, can they draw the product and explain how its carbon chain has changed?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Carboxylic acid derivatives
topics.description: Recognise esters, acyl chlorides, acid anhydrides and amides as derivatives of carboxylic acids in which the –OH is replaced, and compare their reactivity
evidence: Draws and names one example of each derivative
Identifies the group that replaces –OH
Ranks the derivatives by reactivity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown ethanoyl chloride, ethanoic anhydride, ethyl ethanoate and ethanamide, can they explain how each is related to ethanoic acid?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Reactions of acyl chlorides
topics.description: Describe the vigorous reactions of acyl chlorides with water (carboxylic acid), alcohols (esters), ammonia (amides) and amines (N-substituted amides), each releasing HCl, and explain why they are better than carboxylic acids for making esters
evidence: Writes equations for ethanoyl chloride with water, ethanol and ammonia
Explains why HCl fumes are seen
Explains why ester formation from an acyl chloride goes to completion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to make ethyl ethanoate in high yield, can they explain why ethanoyl chloride works better than ethanoic acid?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Nucleophilic addition–elimination
topics.description: Draw the addition–elimination mechanism for an acyl chloride with a nucleophile such as water, an alcohol or ammonia, showing addition to C=O, reformation of C=O and loss of Cl⁻ and H⁺
evidence: Draws the mechanism for ethanoyl chloride and methanol
Explains why the product keeps its C=O group
Identifies the leaving group
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given ethanoyl chloride and ammonia, can they draw the full mechanism?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Acid anhydrides and making aspirin
topics.description: Describe acid anhydrides reacting like acyl chlorides but more slowly, and explain why ethanoic anhydride is preferred industrially, for example in making aspirin from 2-hydroxybenzoic acid
evidence: Writes the equation for ethanoic anhydride with an alcohol
Gives reasons ethanoic anhydride is preferred to ethanoyl chloride
Identifies the ester group formed in aspirin
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why aspirin is made with ethanoic anhydride rather than ethanoyl chloride, can they give at least two reasons?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Amines as bases and nucleophiles
topics.description: Classify amines as primary, secondary or tertiary, explain their basicity using the nitrogen lone pair, and describe making amines from haloalkanes and ammonia, including why mixtures form
evidence: Classifies given amines
Writes the equation for an amine reacting with an acid
Explains why ammonia and a haloalkane give a mixture of amines
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reacts bromoethane with ammonia, can they explain why several amine products form and how to favour ethylamine?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Amides
topics.description: Recognise primary and N-substituted amides, describe their formation from acyl chlorides with ammonia or amines, and identify the amide link in polyamides and proteins
evidence: Draws ethanamide and an N-substituted amide
Writes the equation for forming an amide from an acyl chloride and an amine
Identifies the amide link in a longer molecule
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reacts ethanoyl chloride with methylamine, can they draw and name the product?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Hydrolysis of esters
topics.description: Compare acid hydrolysis of esters (reversible, giving a carboxylic acid and an alcohol) with alkaline hydrolysis (irreversible, giving a carboxylate salt), and apply alkaline hydrolysis of fats to soap making
evidence: Writes equations for acid and alkaline hydrolysis of an ester
Explains why alkaline hydrolysis goes to completion
Describes saponification of a fat
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heats ethyl ethanoate with sodium hydroxide, can they name the products and explain why the reaction does not reverse?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Polyesters and polyamides: synthesis and hydrolysis
topics.description: Draw repeat units of polyesters and polyamides made from diols, diamines and dicarboxylic acids or diacyl chlorides (such as PET and nylon-6,6), and explain their hydrolysis by acids and alkalis and their biodegradability
evidence: Draws the repeat unit from a diamine and a diacyl chloride
Identifies the monomers from a section of polymer
Explains why polyesters and polyamides can be hydrolysed but polyalkenes cannot
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a section of nylon-6,6, can they identify the monomers and explain how it could be broken down?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Nitriles: hydrolysis and reduction
topics.description: Describe hydrolysing nitriles to carboxylic acids and reducing them to primary amines, and use these reactions after adding cyanide to extend a carbon chain
evidence: Writes the equation for hydrolysis of a nitrile
Writes the equation for reduction of a nitrile with [H]
Plans a route that adds one carbon atom to a chain
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert ethanal into 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, can they plan the steps?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Forming carbon–carbon bonds
topics.description: Explain why reactions that make new C–C bonds matter in synthesis, and compare the methods available: cyanide addition or substitution followed by nitrile reactions, and Friedel–Crafts reactions on aromatic rings
evidence: Lists reactions that form new C–C bonds
Explains why most reactions keep the carbon skeleton
Chooses a method to lengthen a chain
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs a product with one more carbon than the starting material, can they choose a reaction that forms a new C–C bond?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Organic practical techniques
topics.description: Use the main organic preparation and purification techniques: heating under reflux, distillation, separating funnel, drying with an anhydrous salt, recrystallisation, and melting-point determination
evidence: Explains when to use reflux and when to distil
Describes how to purify a solid by recrystallisation
Explains how a melting point shows purity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has made an impure solid product, can they describe how to purify it and check its purity?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Functional-group interconversions
topics.description: Build and use a map of conversions between alkanes, alkenes, haloalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, acyl chlorides, amides, amines and nitriles, with reagents and conditions for each step
evidence: Draws a reaction map with reagents on each arrow
Finds a two-step route between functional groups
Identifies conversions that need more than one step
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how to turn propan-1-ol into propanamide, can they use a reaction map to find a route?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Planning multi-step syntheses
topics.description: Plan two- to four-step syntheses by working back from the target (retrosynthesis), choosing reagents and conditions, and judging routes by number of steps, yield, safety and cost
evidence: Works backwards from a target to a starting material
Gives reagents and conditions for each step
Compares two routes and justifies a choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to make propanoic acid from ethene, can they plan a route that adds the extra carbon?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Overall yield and atom economy of a route
topics.description: Calculate the overall yield of a multi-step synthesis by multiplying the yields of each step, and compare routes using atom economy and the number of steps
evidence: Calculates the overall yield of a three-step route
Calculates atom economy for one step
Explains why fewer steps usually give a higher overall yield
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a three-step route with yields of 80%, 70% and 90%, can they find the overall yield and suggest how to improve it?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Identifying an unknown carbonyl compound
topics.description: Identify an unknown carbonyl compound by combining 2,4-DNP, Tollens' or Fehling's results, the melting point of a derivative, and IR and NMR evidence such as the aldehyde proton near δ 9–10
evidence: Plans a sequence of tests
Interprets combined test and spectroscopic results
Explains how each piece of evidence narrows the options
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given test results and spectra for a C₄H₈O compound, can they decide whether it is butanal or butanone?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Shapes of molecules
topics.description: Predict the shapes and bond angles of simple molecules and ions from the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom: linear (180°), trigonal planar (120°), tetrahedral (109.5°), pyramidal (107°) and bent (104.5°)
evidence: Predicts the shape of CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O
Explains why lone pairs reduce bond angles
Draws a tetrahedral carbon with wedge and dash bonds
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked why the bond angle in water is smaller than in methane, can they explain using electron pairs?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Chiral carbon atoms
topics.description: Identify a chiral carbon as one bonded to four different groups, and explain that such a molecule has two non-superimposable mirror-image forms called enantiomers
evidence: Marks the chiral carbon in a structure
Draws the two enantiomers with wedge and dash bonds
Explains why the mirror images cannot be superimposed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given butan-2-ol, can they find the chiral carbon and draw both enantiomers in 3-D?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Optical isomerism and plane-polarised light
topics.description: Explain that enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions, that a racemic mixture gives no overall rotation, and how a polarimeter measures this
evidence: Describes the effect of each enantiomer on plane-polarised light
Explains why a racemic mixture is optically inactive
Describes how a polarimeter is used
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} finds that a sample has no effect on plane-polarised light, can they give two possible explanations?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Racemic products and single-enantiomer medicines
topics.description: Explain that nucleophilic attack on a planar C=O group is equally likely from either side, giving a racemic mixture, and why medicines often need a single enantiomer (as the thalidomide case showed)
evidence: Explains why adding HCN to ethanal gives a racemic product
Explains why enantiomers can have different effects in the body
Describes one way of making a single enantiomer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} makes 2-hydroxypropanenitrile from ethanal, can they explain why the product is optically inactive?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Structure of amino acids
topics.description: Recognise α-amino acids as H₂N–CHR–COOH, with an amine group and a carboxylic acid group on the same carbon and a side chain R that differs between amino acids
evidence: Draws the general structure of an amino acid
Identifies the R group in glycine and alanine
Names an amino acid systematically, such as 2-aminopropanoic acid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown the structure of alanine, can they identify the amine, carboxylic acid and R groups?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Chirality in amino acids
topics.description: Explain that every α-amino acid except glycine has a chiral carbon, and that the amino acids in natural proteins are almost all one enantiomer (the L form)
evidence: Explains why glycine is not chiral
Draws the two enantiomers of alanine
Explains why living things use one enantiomer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares glycine and alanine, can they explain why only alanine has optical isomers?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Amino acids as acids and bases
topics.description: Explain that amino acids react with both acids and bases: in acidic solution the amine group gains H⁺ (–NH₃⁺) and in alkaline solution the carboxylic acid group loses H⁺ (–COO⁻)
evidence: Draws the form of glycine in acid
Draws the form of glycine in alkali
Explains which group reacts in each case
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} adds hydrochloric acid to glycine, can they draw the ion formed?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Zwitterions and the isoelectric point
topics.description: Explain that amino acids exist as zwitterions (H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻) at their isoelectric point, and use this to explain their high melting points and solubility in water
evidence: Draws the zwitterion of an amino acid
Explains why amino acids are crystalline solids with high melting points
Defines the isoelectric point
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told glycine melts at over 200 °C while ethanoic acid melts at 17 °C, can they explain the difference?

topics.subject: Science
topics.name: Separating amino acids by charge
topics.description: Explain how amino acids carry different charges at a given pH and so move differently in an electric field (electrophoresis), with no movement at the isoelectric point
evidence: Predicts the charge of an amino acid above and below its isoelectric point
